This is an early access review before the first update.
I have completed the game after roughly 25 hours of playtime. 

Positives: 
- The NPC's bring a nice change to people who want to play this game but dont have the friends to do so.
- Graphically looks beautiful. Especially with the changing seasons.
- A ton of weapon options.
- The build mode has taken a huge improvement over the original.
- Combat feels better than the original. (Minus the handgun, it feels really weird to use)
- The new weather system really does help the world feel more alive.
- The 3D printer is a VERY good addition. It adds a sort of "shop" feel. But I feel we need more options in this printer.
- The sled is a TON of fun.
- The addition of peaceful mode allows this game to be accessible to anyone. 
- The addition of a GPS is VERY appreciated and makes navigation much easier.
- Sharing / passing inventory items to coop members is a huge improvement for teamwork.


Negatives:
- A very lacking world. Theres like 7 animals on the entire island. Deer, Moose, Squirrel, Rabbit, Turtle, and Bird, and fish.
- The story is somehow even more bare-bones than the original. The only means to progress the story is through emails that you can find printed out around the island. Theres also literally only one line of dialogue in the entire game. At that point, why even have it? Everyone just gestures and makes grunts instead of talking. 
- There are multiple caves that are completely empty and serve next to no purpose outside of providing minor resources.
- The caves that arent instant dead-ends feel shorter and less dynamic compared to the original. (For example, in the original you were using the climbing axe to navigate an extremely deep cave.) 
- Not all of the original mutations are in this game. And the mutations that are in this game are nowhere as threatening as the original. The only real threat is in the final lab where you fight the final mutation because its very fast and does 2 armor per hit.
- The ending is absolutely horrible. It drops SUPER abruptly. There isnt a final boss or big fight at the end. Its just a really big room with about 20 or so of the final mutation. Which can be easily handled with the cross. 


Bugs:
- Rotten food can still be cooked and it will turn into "cooked" food which can be eaten like normal.
- The GPS tracker does not use any of the custom icons. They will default always to the radio icon regardless of what you chose.
- Virginia can sometimes just disappear and cannot be found. Im not sure what causes this to happen but it seems to be random.
- Kalvin's AI is hilariously bad. For every one correct thing he does, he breaks three other things. Hes just a liability and youre better off telling him to just stay in rest til the end of the game so that you can get the achievement. I feel he would serve a better purpose being able to help you in combat like with Virginia.
- Multiple achievements are bugged / do not work correctly in multiplayer. 
- If you are building and get attacked by a cannibal, the structure gets bugged and will not let you build on to it anymore.
- Multiple items will get stuck to your hand when hit in the middle of an animation. Stuff as minor as weapon visual bugs or something major like being hit while picking up a cannibal body will just have a cannibals butt in your face until you leave the game. 
- Sometimes coop player's will not show up on the map. But they are visible on the overworld. 


Minor complaints: 
- Deer absolutely BOOK it. I get that this is to encourage the "stealth" but they will hear a leaf and just instantly run to a different zip code. This makes hunting deer in the early game next to impossible. Compared to the original where they will stop running to give you a chance to catch up and take them down with the axe.
- Speaking of stealth, this mechanic serves next to no purpose at all. Cannibals and mutants will still spot you even if youre crouched in a bush. 
- Base building is basically unessential. The best way to play this game is being as nomadic as possible. Settling down will just get you invaded by cannibals. And you dont really need a place to store your food and resources because the game lets you hold an incredible amount just on your back. And with crates and boxes littered all over the island you are almost always good on resources.
- You are able to give weapons to Virginia but you have to give YOUR weapons. There are multiple spawn locations for the handgun and the shotgun. But you cannot carry more than one at the same time. This makes it incredibly annoying trying to give your weapons to her. Let us hold the other guns so that we can give them to Virginia later. (Just like how we cant equip any of the Kelvin / Virginia clothing.)
- The NPCs do not follow you into any cave. While I get its somewhat harder to program, they would be a bigger help in the caves as that is where youre going to spend MOST of your fighting. 
- It would be nice to have a crafting book, similar to the survival guide book. Basically asking for the option to fast craft previously unlocked recipes. It would also be nice to let us craft in bulk. So that we dont have to rewatch the animation each time.
- Unless im mistaken, firewood serves next to no purpose. It just sits there and looks pretty but you cannot use it.
- The game does not tell you that the GPS can be zoomed out and zoomed in with middle mouse. This is a HUGE improvement over the standard GPS size. 
- Not being able to like full screen the map and have a clear and full view over the entire island. The best you can get is a 1/3rd view. You also cannot have a compass so it is somewhat easy to lose your way around unless you use a third-party map service.
- The turtle shell serves no purpose at all. This was used in the original as a way to collect rain water but that recipe is not currently in the game.
- There is no penalty for not eating/drinking/sleeping outside of a lower stamina bar.
- There is no penalty for eating raw/rotten/poison food. Your character will just cough and then shake it off immediately. 
- The garden plot is only used for one plant at a time. Which is hilariously bad compared to the original. 
- The shovel is ONLY used for story progression / minor loot spots. I was hoping that this could be used for land excavation / setting up traps.
- The mountain serves no purpose aside from just being fun to sled off of. Theres no items, enemies, or animals all over the area. Its completely barren and devoid of meaning. 
- The shark is hilariously under powered. Really making it an ACHIEVEMENT to die by it. Because they bite you once and run away and the bite is WAY too minimal on damage. It took about 20 minutes of just annoying this shark to die by it. 

Suggestions: 
- We dont need 3 different Axes if they all serve the same purpose with minimal stat changes. Either make the axes have a MUCH wider stat range, or give them unique interactions with the world.
- Please add more animals. Maybe even some hostile ones like bears or something. 
- Winter is the only season that brings a survival change. It makes you manage your heat but I hardly noticed a difference of being cold outside of a minor stamina penalty. Maybe include a sickness for ignoring this warning. And let us craft medicine using some of the healing plants. 
- On a similar note, we should include a survival change with summer as well. Maybe have us dehydrate faster or something.
- Please bring back the original mutations and add more.

Overall: 
This game has a ton of potential to be a true successor to the original. 
While I get this is early access, I feel this is EARLY early access. Its just way too soon to genuinely play this game.
Unless youre just in it for the base building and just being in a pretty world.
In its current state, this is a 6/10 game. Its worth getting if you just really enjoyed the original, but this does really need more time in the oven to truly become a 10/10.

Since no one with a positive review is willing to explain why, I guess I will.

          Right off the bat, visually, this game is jaw-droppingly phenomenal. The lighting, presentation, and atmosphere has been brilliantly re-captured to ensure older fans from the first game feel like they are returning to somewhere that feels oddly familiar, yet holds many new and unique encounters we have yet to discover. The colors, especially the greens, pop in just the right way to further emphasize the seemingly calm and collected forest during the day that can quickly change into a dark and unsettling nightmare by night.

	Endnight has again hit the nail on the head with the combat. Considering the old system of charging up momentum to land attacks worked exceptionally well, it's understandable they did not try and reinvent the wheel. Combat has been expanded and smoothed out just enough to keep it feeling fun, fresh and different. Landing hits is just as satisfying as it was in the old game, and mastering these techniques is especially entertaining with both new enemies and their original, upgraded counterparts. 

	As far as interaction mechanics, the inventory system has been cleverly improved, and Kelvin is a genuinely cool addition to the game. For other friendless losers such as myself, having Kelvin around is good company. Interacting with him is intuitive and straightforward, and losing track of him isn't a problem with the GPS you get right off the bat. Starting off with some way to orient yourself in a map that's five times bigger than the first game is also a welcome change. The "quick inventory" while you're on the move is a welcome upgrade as well. The crafting menu has also been improved, separating custom buildings from presets, which makes it easier to keep track of what you can make using custom buildings. Unfortunately, the garbage control scheme returns so for the first five minutes into my new save I was making the game playable instead of... playing the game.

	But holy smokes the building is 1000% better than the first game. You still have your already mentioned presets for use in a pinch, and you have the massively improved custom building. Instead of laying out where you want everything to go all at once, you get to pick and choose as you create your desired structure, which makes it way easier to manage your resources while making it, and also allows you to make changes as you see fit. This is a huge step up from the previous game, and it's great.

	I see some complaints with the performance but I personally had no issues. With the medium preset my game ran at a rock solid 75-80 fps, which is perfectly fine for a game like this. Survival games don't need absurdly high frame-rates; what's more important is certainly the frame times and consistency. And my game would rarely drop frames, it again stayed at 76-77 fps with little deviation.

	I think that's really this game in a nutshell. The first game, but with pretty much every mechanic getting upgraded and reworked in a positive way (for the most part). There's some reused sound FX throughout the game which I thought was a little disappointing, but there have to be some expectations with a team of just 30 people. People get wrapped up in the fact that visually it competes with triple-A games, but those same people forget a tiny team of 30 put this together, and they are only asking for 30 bucks, which is a steal for a game with this much visual fidelity and replayability. Not to mention the oncoming free updates that will only add more content. It's certainly okay to be critical of a product and point out its flaws, but with expectations in check, this comes out as a pretty solid game.

Sons of the Forest is a great game there is no doubt about that, and if you feel like you want to play the game then by all means go ahead, I did and I enjoyed it, but if ever there was a time to wait for a game to come out of Early Access it would be now. As someone who enjoyed The Forest far more than I could have expected I had very high expectation for Sons of the Forest, but sadly I think SOTF is just not there yet, and here’s why…

1 – The Island
From what I’ve been able to gather is seems that the general consensus is that SOTF’s map is roughly 5 times bigger than that of The Forest, but bigger isn’t always better. I don’t recall a single time in The Forest when I felt like I was losing out on anything because I had to travel across the map. Though the map was much smaller, it was balanced for the amount of content the game offered and nothing was ever really “too far” away. At this point in time there just isn’t enough content in SOTF to justify such a large map. Surprisingly there are about half as many caves as there were in The Forest, at least for the time being, of course they’ve added bunkers but even then we only get a handful. Don’t get me wrong, the game looks AMAZING, but when everything is so far away that it takes you half an hour to run across the map it will eventually start to wear on you.

2 – The Caves
One of the most iconic aspects of The Forest was its intricate intertwining cave system that could be easily accessed from almost any part of the map thanks to its many cave entrances. You could venture into the darkness and emerge almost anywhere on the map depending on how far you went, this made everything feel connected and really helped tie the islands overworld together with its cave system. Not only that but finding certain equipment could help you dive even further into the depths of darkness which in turn upped the danger levels as you delved further and further… well, this is gone now. In SOTF each cave is its own standalone cave, many times with the exit being only a few meters away from its entrance. Not only that but most of the times the caves don’t really pose any type of threat, either they’re completely empty and you can just run through them, or they’re filled to the brim with mutants and you can still just run right through them because there’s nothing limiting your progress through the caves. Worst of all is that most of the caves in SOTF just aren’t memorable, I feel the reason for this is mostly because after looting a cave there’s really no reason to come back, you get the main loot from the cave and that’s it, that cave is done and you never have to visit it again which sucks.

3 – The Survival
While this might be a bug and unintentional, as the game stands now it allows you to re-loot absolutely everything in the game, suitcases included, making it so you never have to worry about running out of supplies. Now I know that this was also a thing in The Forest, but it only applied to items in caves and some very basic overworld items (yet another reason you don’t need to return to the caves). That and the many duplication glitches that currently plague the game make it so you never really have to worry about survival. Wanna build a house? You can build a mansion by just chopping down one tree and using a stick. Ran out of ammo/grenades/crafting materials? Just save and reload next to a camp as many times as you need till you top off everything. Also, did I mention that the end-game armor is infinite? That’s right, you will never run out of armor, and even the best armor can be fully crafted early to mid-game after restarting a few times in the correct bunker. Not to mention that our friend Kelvin offers a never-ending supply of fish so you’ll never go hungry again. Basically, you never have to worry about surviving in this game, hell you don’t even need a base, everything you need will fit in your backpack, and even if you do go hungry or get thirsty you don’t really get punished for doing so. 

4 – The Story
This is probably what hurt the most for me, while The Forest didn’t have much of a story per se, once you reached the end you got enough of an explanation for everything to make sense. In SOTF however, the ending is so bizarre and non-sensical that it just leaves you confused as to who everyone is and where they came from. It wasn’t until I went onto Youtube and found someone who put in the time to do the detective work and piece everything together that I was finally able to understand a bit, and even then, it was just an interpretation of the events that happened, you really have to stretch your imagination for everything to make sense.

Now don’t get me wrong, in spite of all of these issues I’m fully aware that the game is in early access and thus not complete, and while I did enjoy the experience during my first playthrough I can’t help but think of all the possibilities of how much more the game can improve during this early access phase and how I could have had a much more enjoyable experience in a complete game, because you only get one chance at a first playthrough. Sons of the Forest has all the potential to surpass The Forest, but as the game stands it just isn’t there yet.

Super immersive sandbox horror survival game with tons to do and hours of gameplay to sink into. The building mechanics are amazing, and the NPC characters really add to the creepy atmosphere. They’re not just there for show they actually make the world feel alive, and always get you looking over your shoulder.

Sons of the Forest is a solid survival game with strong mechanics and one standout feature that sets it apart from most others. The atmosphere. Not just the visuals or the enemies. The sound design is what makes this game terrifying in the best way.

The caves are where it hits hardest. Not because something jumps out at you. But because of what you hear. Crackling rocks. Distant echoes. The sound of something moving just out of reach. That tension builds without a single enemy on screen. The fear comes from the sound alone. You stop moving. Not because of a cutscene or scripted event. You stop because your instincts tell you something is wrong. The game creates dread with almost nothing.

Above ground the game looks great. The forest is dense and feels alive. Building is detailed and hands on. You place logs and supports yourself. It feels like you are building something that matters. Combat is improved from the first game. Enemies react more. They test your defenses. They back off when hurt. It still has bugs but the behavior feels better overall.

It is not perfect, but in its best moments, it does something most games fail to do. It makes you pause, not because you have to, but because you are actually afraid to keep going. That is real tension. That is what makes it worth playing.

This game has achieved something no other "survival crafting" game has, the vibe.
It is not a grind for materials, not a perk chase, not a find something way to advanced too early and the list goes on.
It is a live in the woods game, a fortify your home game, a fear the locals and hope to make it through the night game. On top of all that it has an mysterious plot that you have to piece together through exploration. 
Some will say the map is empty and there is nothing to do. Well those people might play a little too much of other games that have events or seasons or battle passes. 
I applaud the developers of this game for making the best building system I've ever seen. You simply pick up a log or stone a place it where you want it. Piece by piece, slowly creating your own masterpiece or being frustrated as you try to learn how to essentially construct real housing.
Survival feels so real as well. Hunting requires patience and practice. You need to skin the animals and forage plants for meaningful recipes. All while maintaining your firewood supply and simultaneously pissing off the locals. Water needs to be clean, boil it or find a fresh source. Sleep well and make breakfast in the morning or wake up depleted in the middle of the night and defend your ability to sleep at all. 
Combat is simple yet rewarding. Swing an axe and hope to connect but poor timing means you get hit as well. Armor yourself with different material, learn to block and stave off being cannibalized for a few more hits. Make and find weapons to add range and power to your attacks. Enemies have lives and meaning. They aren't just looking for you to kill, They are living their life and you showed up or they found you. 

Too Long Didn't Read: Simply the best stranded on an island and living the simple life game out there. Chop trees make man happy.

TLDR:
A pretty good survival game with fun building, survival mechanics, traps, helper NPCs, etc. Decent combat, with maybe a bit too much power given to the players, and a story that didn't pan out very well. A decent survival game with some good things going for it, though not as strong as it's predecessor where it counts. 7/10

The good:
The visuals are much better and the level design felt more rich. The forests feel properly dense and good to navigate. The new building system is better to work, allowing for much more specific manual control to let you engage in more nuanced construction. The inclusion of friendly NPCs was a welcome addition and it worked fairly well. The game ran well with fairly high settings and I played through the whole game with 2 friends and we never suffered a networking or connectivity issue.

The less good:
There were some balancing issues, the more obvious one was the deep inclusion of firearms that make mowing through groups a bit too easy, especially when playing with multiple players. The less obvious balancing issue was the golf cart. When you get at least a bit of speed with the golf cart, it will one-shot most living things in the game. Not necessarily an issue in of itself, but the fact that we found not 1, but 3 golf carts in the first couple hours of gameplay meant that we could just mow down an entire camp, pilfer all the valuables, and drive off and do it again. It basically allowed us to skip the early game difficulty when you are supposed to be more poorly equipped. Though admittedly, driving through dense forest and swerving between trees while blaring techno music was quite a vibe.
The story was a bit less coherent than the first. The build up to the end was fine as they are very shortcoming with the details, forcing you to piece it together yourself, helping with the mystery of it all. The main issue is when you get the final details and put the final pieces of the story together, it doesn't amount to much of anything. Also I agree with my friend who felt like the final boss was "a wet fart", resulting in a disappointing conclusion of the game.

Bought this game and played it way too much over winter break and had a ton of fun that being said we'll do a pros and cons list. We'll start with cons.
#1: Building can get tedious and has some annoying rules.
#2: AI feels weird at times. A group of cannibals are staring at you and you shoot their friend with an arrow and they don't immediately attack you or run away from you. It can feel strange.
#3: Story is rather short and hard to piece together.
#4: Once you have all the weapons in the game you feel a little op.
#5: In some situations the amount of enemies feels lacking.
(I've heard some people complaining there are way too many enemies but I have not experienced this.)
#6: Combat isn't too special as you simply slash, block, parry or shoot.
Now onto the pros.
#1: Atmosphere and setting are great. You really get the feeling of a dangerous, mysterious island and the dense forest makes it hard to know when you will be attacked.
#2: Massive open world map. You can go anywhere and build anywhere you want and while walking can get tedious various game mechanics to alleviate this are in-place.
#3: Building is SOO much fun. From building spike walls to giant houses or waterfall fortresses to mansions on a lake or great walls of china you can let you're imagination run wild and build whatever you want. I had that same feeling I had years ago playing Minecraft building whatever I want when I was a kid.
#4: As previous stated combat isn't special but it is fun. Dodging, slicing and parrying with swords, chopping and blocking with axes, shooting with bows and slingshots (Slingshots btw, lol) and shooting creepy crawllies with guns is all a lot of fun anyways.
#5: The variety of enemies is great. While you do eventually get used to them all, the variety of cannibals you fight and the variety of mutants makes this interesting and scary.
#6: The quirks and interactions from the AI with you and each other are fun and interesting.
#7: The survival aspect of needing/gathering food and water and creating shelter is present without being annoying.
#8: Highly customization. The settings and well as ability to create custom games with custom difficulties for individual aspects is great.
#9: You have a personal helper who follows you around who you can tell to do all the annoying stuff you don't want to do.
#10: The island really feels alive with animals weather and changing seasons, each bringing unique challenges and advantages.
#11: Good mods. Game does not have a steam workshop at time of review but the mods on other websites I've found have been virus free, (however still use caution as all downloads and websites have potential for malware) and been high quality, quirky add-ons or QOL improvements.
#12: Game feels appropriately gory and violent for the setting and situation without feeling over the top, forced, or exaggerated.
#13: Game doesn't use cheap jump scares to scare you it lets the monster and atmosphere naturally do it.
#14: Reliable, easy to use incredibly fun multiplayer.
#15: Lots of tutorials to help you if you get stuck,
#16: The music is great.
Random note: It feels very satisfying cutting downs trees in this game. Undoing all of Mr Beast's work is actually kinda fun.
And finally a feature I'm going to call neutral: An easy to use command console. Some people may hate it because it allows the potential for "cheating" and it ruins the survival experience. Some may love it as a means to focus on building or adventuring or survival or whatever it is you want out of this game. Also you can choose just, not to use it. Do not be fooled by websites that say you need to download their special "unlocker mod" or whatever to access the console, you do not. It is completely default within the game.

Sons of the Forest doesn’t feel like a typical survival game. It feels raw. Wild. Personal. From the moment you crash-land on that island, the game drops all pretense and just lets you exist in it. You’re not being guided. You’re not being handheld. You’re alone, cold, and immediately in danger. But somehow, that danger feels real in a way few games manage.

The forest is alive in a way that creeps up on you. Trees sway with the wind, shadows stretch across the dirt, animals roam freely, and then there’s silence. Real, heavy silence. Sometimes you’ll hear breathing that isn’t yours. Or see movement in the distance that you hope was just wind. Everything in the world responds to you, but nothing caters to you. There’s something deeply unsettling about that.

Building in this game is incredibly satisfying. It’s not about dropping pre-made blueprints and watching walls appear. You’re cutting down actual trees, splitting logs by hand, laying each piece down yourself. Structures feel earned. Even a simple shelter feels like a project. Over time, you start to take pride in what you’ve made. Not because it’s pretty, but because you bled to protect it.

Combat is tough. Every swing matters. Every shot has weight. Enemies don’t charge blindly. They watch. They test you. Some scream to call others. Some creep behind you without a sound. And some just stand at the edge of the woods and stare until you do something about it. It makes you hesitate. It makes you paranoid. And it works.

You’re not completely alone, though. Kelvin is your companion, injured and silent. He can’t talk but he helps. He gathers materials, follows your commands, and sometimes just sits and rests when he’s overwhelmed. There’s something deeply human about him. Then there’s Virginia. She doesn’t take orders. She observes. Eventually, if she trusts you, she’ll help. She’ll bring you food. She’ll fight alongside you. And when she does, it’s not just useful. It’s emotional.

The island changes constantly. Weather, seasons, even the tone of the game shifts over time. Winter isn’t just a visual effect. It’s survival on hard mode. Food disappears. Animals vanish. Water freezes. Everything becomes still. The sense of isolation hits harder than any enemy ever could.

The story unfolds slowly and without much explanation. You’ll find bodies. Mysterious bunkers. Technology that doesn’t belong in the woods. You’ll piece together what happened, if you care to look. It never interrupts you. It just waits for you to dig deeper. The horror comes not from jump scares, but from slowly realizing the truth behind what you're seeing.

Playing with others turns this all into something completely different. You can build massive compounds together. You can split up and get lost. You can survive as a team or fall apart in the face of chaos. It’s messy. It’s unpredictable. And it’s endlessly engaging.

There are moments of quiet that hit harder than any action scene. Sitting by a fire while rain falls around you. Watching Kelvin rest while your shelter creaks in the wind. Catching a glimpse of Virginia dancing in the distance like she’s forgotten what the world is.

Sons of the Forest is not easy. It’s not polished in the traditional sense. But that’s exactly why it’s so memorable. It’s uncomfortable. It’s rewarding. It’s dangerous in a way that makes you lean in. There’s no flair. No filler. Just survival in its purest form.

The first Forest game was a one of a kind game that I put quite a bit of hours into exploring the island and building structures and cowering in the corner while cannibals ravaged my base. This one expands upon that experience in every way and does an even better job.

Especially regarding the building mechanic, this game has the most detailed building system I think I've ever seen in a game, which makes it real fun to make whatever structure you want the way you specifically want it. It can be a bit tedious if I'm being honest, but I've never personally had a problem with that since I enjoy the manual work of chopping the trees down and then the individual logs into the size I need. One thing I will say that got kinda annoying with the building, is that a bunch of the blueprints require all different kinds of wood sizes, some of which are only small parts of the log, which means that afterward you're left with a whole ton of leftover cut logs that you can't really use for anything else unless you're building a blueprint that specifically requires whatever it is you have an abundance of, and even then, you're typically still left with some. I had so many different log pieces at once before that I wasn't even able to walk out the door of my house lol. With that said, I for one am really fond of building and decorating within games, and if you truly wanted to, you could play this game purely for that reason and play it as nothing more than a building sim.

Most people likely aren't going to buy this game purely for the building system though, which brings us to the survival and horror aspect of the game. If you're not a builder and don't care about spending 20 hours building a 3 story cabin on a small island in the center of a lake with a fully furnished houseboat that can't even go anywhere due to the fact the lake only leads to a waterfall... then the exploration and surviving side of the game is super fun too. Now I've seen a lot of people complain that the map is actually *too* big (which isn't a complaint you typically hear) and that it isn't filled with enough stuff for it to justify the fact the game area is very big, but honestly, I never once had those same thoughts. In fact, I would get distracted often while exploring just because I'd keep finding stuff, whether that was a cave or a bunker, cannibal camp, some other odd area, or even a pretty area (the environment is gorgeous). There is a lot to find and to do, and I feel that the people who complain about the "empty" map are the same type of people that complain that Elden Ring is "empty" just because it doesn't have something at every step. And it's not like it's difficult to traverse the map either when the game gives you multiple means of transportation such as the golf cart, the knight V, or even the hang glider which can get you across the map in a minute.

Back to the main point though; if you want a solid survival experience, where not only does the cannibals and other unimaginable horrors pose a threat, but also your food, thirst, and sleep bar, then this is the game for you.  There was genuinely many times where our worst enemy wasn't the insane cannibals running around the forest, but the fact that we didn't carry any MRE's or energy drinks with us (my friend had to eat raw cat food once and I think I ate a human leg...). And don't forget about the temperature! There are seasons within the game, and winter is easily the most deadly. Not only will you freeze on the surface and within caves (which can screw you over when you have zero stamina to go up against a mutant, true story), but it will also freeze water, so fun fact: that little island in the center of a lake that you chose to build at specifically because you thought it was safe, is no longer safe. Hope you built walls, otherwise prepare to get raided every night by your local crack addicts and chernobyl victims.

This game is amazing for multi-player, there is plenty of fun to be had and moments to experience. But don't worry if you are playing single player, the game has two NPCs that you can befriend and have stick around you. One of which, is Kelvin, which serves as a substitute for another player. You can order him around and have him gather stuff for you, build stuff for you, protect your base, or just follow you around while holding a radio :). Kelvin is great, Kelvin is the best, we all love Kelvin. There is also Virginia which is a multi-limbed mutated lady, and while you unfortunately *can't* give her tasks, you *can* give her a shotgun and a pistol at the same time which she will duel wield and use to protect your base from any enemies. Loved seeing that the first time we figured that out.

Speaking of enemies, in case it wasn't obvious yet, there are mutants and cannibals inhabiting the island you're on. The game is a horror game, and there are some genuinely unsettling moments I've experienced during it. The caves by themselves are horrifying, it's claustrophobic, dark, you *know* there's stuff down there with you, but you are forced to bear through it if you want to progress through the main story of the game (which I'll get to in a minute). But it's not like the surface is any better, I've been chased by cannibals while flooring it as fast as I could in a golf cart, I've been jumped by cannibals in the pitch dark that were hiding in trees, they even stalk you which is terrifying to see at the beginning. They'll hide in bushes, trees, behind rocks, peek at you behind things, run up to you and sprint away. You aren't safe anywhere. With that being said, once you get weapons and armor and begin to understand how the enemies work, they sort of lose the fear factor and you instead just become the Doom Slayer and tear through them. Still very fun though, but if you're looking for a true horror experience all the way through, then maybe not the right game.

One other main thing I wanna bring up is the storyline/plot of the game. I have... zero clue what it is, it is extremely convoluted and weird if I'm being honest. I tried to piece together what was happening through the letters and notes you'd find, and from the world building, and I thought I had a grasp on it until somehow a [spoiler]literal futuristic alien society was introduced at the end of the game where you catch a glimpse of some sort of realm through a portal.[/spoiler] ...I don't know, I didn't know where the story was heading but I certainly didn't expect *that*. I'm sure the story makes sense... somehow, but it just seems very odd fitting and random for the gameplay and themes. For the most part, we just ignored the story in favor of the gameplay, which is what I imagine most people do.

That's all the main things I have to say, some other small notes is that the graphics are beautiful and so is the environment, if you love realism, you'll love this game. And the game runs very well, I had no lag issues whatsoever, however I believe my friend did have some problems during the times it would rain but, I had no issue with that even though I have the lesser PC build. One miscellaneous thing I didn't like was the proximity chat mic quality, it was so bad that we turned it off and just used discord (which is unfortunate because proximity chat is one of the best features of modern gaming). It'd also be nice if the developers were more interactive with their community and gave more information on whether the game is still being updated or not. And I understand that game developers don't owe us anything, but still, it's good courtesy to let your consumers know what's going on, no?

Anyway, those are my thoughts on the game. I definitely recommend this game, especially if you're looking for a good experience with friends. I've always loved The Forest, and this is exactly how I imagined the first one should have been. Buy it full price or on sale, it's worth it either way.

After 200+ hours, I can confidently say Sons of the Forest is one of the most immersive and rewarding survival experiences out there.

The building system? Incredibly satisfying. The AI? Genuinely smart and sometimes terrifying. The world? Gorgeous, brutal, and full of secrets. Whether I'm base-building, fending off mutants, or exploring the depths of a creepy cave with a flashlight and bad decisions, the game constantly keeps me engaged.

Even after all this time, I’m still finding new ways to survive, create, and (occasionally) scream like a child.

If you love survival games, stunning visuals, and just the right amount of chaos — this forest has your name carved into a tree.

This is pretty much the best a survival game can get. 
The game drops you onto a cannibal and mutant infested island and gives you the complete freedom to do whatever you'd like. It can be pretty tough at times, but you are able to customize your difficulty in whatever way makes it a more enjoyable experience for you. You can change enemy health, how much damage, indestructible structures, and tons more.

The graphics are beautiful, and the attention to detail is top tier. 
The seasons change. Summer is bright, green and lush until you get to slowly see the leaves change color, Certain crops stop growing and eventually snow begins to fall. You leave a path in the snow where you walk. Freshwater lakes freeze. The amount of small, more obscure realistic physics I noticed while playing was amazing. It really feels like the devs thought of even the tiny things that don't matter much but increase the immersion a ton.

The story is optional. 
If you just wanna survive on the island forever, build a massive base, you can do that. However, I found uncovering all the clues and the mystery extremely exciting and interesting, especially after playing the original The Forest.

If I had to make one complaint, although a very minor one - it would be that certain, small areas of the map feel a bit empty. But this is contrasted by the amount of things to do, and other portions of the map that are very well done and fleshed-out. So trust me, do not let this deter you from playing the game as this is simply me just nitpicking.

There are very few survival games who knock it out of the park the way Endnight Games does. 
I have a lot of trust in them, and am really hoping for a 3rd installment of this series. This has easily become my favorite survival game, and easily in my top 10 games of all time. It's just a must-have experience for gamers. Very much worth the purchase.
If your computer can handle it, it's one of the best games I've ever played; but it's more fun with friends.

I don’t just “like” this game. I don’t just “play” this game. Sons of the Forest is not entertainment—it is a spiritual experience. It is my North Star. My life compass. My emotional support cannibal simulator.

When I first booted it up, I thought, “Haha cool survival game, cut down some trees, build a house, maybe eat some berries.” WRONG. This game grabbed me by the throat, kissed my forehead, and then drop-kicked me into the abyss of obsession. I dream in logs now. I hear the phantom buzzing of my chainsaw when I close my eyes. If I step outside in real life and see a tree, my first thought is: That’s free real estate.

The cannibals? They don’t scare me anymore. They complete me. Every time they scream at me, my serotonin levels spike like I just mainlined pure happiness. I used to be afraid of the caves, but now I wander them like some kind of deranged bat, licking the walls for stamina regen. When I find mutants lurking in the shadows, I whisper: “Take me, daddy,” and sprint at them with a torch like a maniac.

Kelvin? My sweet, sweet Kelvin. He is both my son, my brother, my emotional crutch, and my legally wedded spouse. He stares at me with that blank, golden retriever gaze, and I know peace. “Take logs,” I tell him, and he waddles off with the determination of a saint carrying humanity’s sins. If Kelvin dies, I die. End of story.

And Virginia… oh, Virginia. Three arms, three legs, and somehow, three times the charm. When she sprints into battle with a pistol in one hand, a shotgun in the other, and her ballet shoes covered in mud, I feel things no therapist can unpack. Forget romance. Forget marriage. I want a tax break with Virginia.

The game punishes me, breaks me, humiliates me—
and yet I keep coming back like a worm squirming for the hook.
I freeze to death in winter. I starve because I forgot to cook my leg meat. I get jumped by a mutant while trying to admire the sunset. And every time I respawn in a cannibal camp, I think: Yes. More. Please.

Sons of the Forest is not just a survival game. It is a psychological thriller. It is a horror movie. It is a love story. It is a second job that doesn’t pay me, ruins my mental health, and yet fills the gaping void in my heart.

10/10.
I would chainsaw my real-life furniture to craft a log cabin if Steam asked me to.
I would marry Kelvin and Virginia in a three-way ceremony officiated by a cannibal wearing bone armor.
I would let a mutant crawl into my chest cavity and live there rent free.

This game is pain. This game is love.
And I will never uninstall.

Sons of the Forest is the 'early access' release of the sequel to the much lauded Endnight debut, The Forest (2018) and is a complete sideways improvement. Nearly everything that The Forest does, 2023's Sons of the Forest improves upon in almost every field. Animation quality and variety are both numerous and exquisitely visualised if somewhat superfluous, the graphics and environmental production tower over anything in The Forest and the audio work is first rate with a killer soundtrack and ambient sound design that brings the rainforest to life. The excellent and satisfying melee combat of the original makes a return.
Where The Forest explored themes of isolation, body horror and fear (with a sprinkling of b-movie mystic shlock) 'Sons' relegates these horror themes to the back seat, with the emphasis being on shooting guns and big budget set pieces. Both films are loving pastiches of the genre pieces they take their inspiration from. The workmanlike and DIY production and direction of the original Forest has been replaced by a slicker, glossier production that wants you tobe some badass action movie star. However, the pace of the game is ironically quicker in the first game due to the smaller size and tighter plot of the original than it is in this more or less straightforward survival game.
However, as technically brilliant and graphically superior as Sons is, it is where we make the comparisons to the gameplay of the The Forest that we can see the glaring deficiencies in actual game experience and content. The Forest had an organic sense of progression in terms of plot, exploration and reward, whereas Sons leads the player to the new locales in a much more linear fashion with progression being rewarded with ammunition and animations. The original had a forest that was deep in spite of its small size, extensively detailed with each part of the world map given its own character and environmental design, whereas Sons feels like a map that is admittedly more convincing as a real world location but suffers from its own size. There are simply too few points of interest for a map this size and the locations that do exist are barely worth exploring. The Forest had caves that each felt different and each had a character to them, places that really needed to be scouted, prepared for and deliberately explored, not just a place to go to because we needed a key item, or that there wasnt much else to do but go and actually explore them. The Forest felt alive with malice - Endnight paying homage to the largely Italian-made cannibal exploitation films of the late seventies (Cannibal Holocaust, Cannibal Ferox, et al), yet Sons really just leans into how realistic the forest is as its main feature. There a few grisly props lying about, but there are no eviscerated japanese businessmen or plane crash survivors strung up, just a few faceless mooks impaled upon sticks here and there, which in itself does not lend itself to much emotional connection to the game and oh boy, we will get to that....
Instead of placing you in the shoes of plane crash survivor Eric LeBlanc, protagonist of The Forest, tasked with finding his abducted son Timmy, Sons establishes that you are a member of a PMC group, an operative sent with a mission to go and discover or recover the family of billionaire capitalist Edward Puffton. Without going into too much detail, there is a definite tonal shift in both approach and presentation of the main plot. In the Forest, Timmy is your emotional connection to the world, the driving force behind the plot and the general atmosphere of the game is one of horror and fear. Sons of the Forest had you down as Action Man, you shoot guns, have things with 'tactical' in their name and you have a straightforward mission. There was a plane crash subplot in The Forest which tasks you with tracking down exactly what happened to the survivors, some of whom surviving one catastrophe to be rewarded with an even more unfortunate end. Now in Sons of the Forest there are a few corpses strewn about the place, faceless operators we couldnt give a toss about. There are no cues or environmental story telling as to how they met their end or who was behind this. Just some impaled tacticool guys. And that is our emotional payoff on discovery of what happened to our mercenary comrades. 
Now, Sons approaches its emotional commitments differently. The Forest has you exploring the game trying to rescue your child and escape the island, there is an established connection between a likeable player character and his mission. He at least has a name, a noble goal and is armed only with his expertise in fieldcraft and an emergency exit axe. Sons however allows to develop your emotional connection in a more organic fashion by ones relation with the only other survivor of the heli crash, Kelvin. It also introduces us to Virginia, who almost becomes something as a surrogate for the Timmy emotional connection by way of character interaction. This is a departure, but a welcome and sophisticated piece of game design. But the sophistication is only skin deep, Kelvin carries logs, Ginnie shoots things. So if youre not into building, Kelvin doesnt factor into the game (I tell him to hide at the heli crash to be shot of him) and if youre more interested in discovering the true depth of the AI NPCs by playing in a non hostile, observational style, Ginnie will make sure the full range of AI behaviour becomes locked to hostility by shooting up the place. One of the standout features of the original was the apparent depth of player interaction with the NPCs who populated the peninsular, be that in either non violent or hostile interactions and this has been improved upon by Sons of the Forest, but nothing that is present here was not present in The Forest. Only the sophistication of its presentation. As a side note, Endnight has introduced two new player companions and a deeper AI system, but couldnt implement an insanity system that would create interesting gameplay scenarios? For all the imagination that Endnight have put into both games, surely there must an idea unscooped from a brain cell somewhere in the office.
The reason the emotional connection is important is because people remember and empathise the triumph of Eric LeBlanc in The Forest. We will probably remember seeing the twinkle of life in Kelvins eyes as we resuscitate him or the first time we watch a impromptu ballet recital from Virginia but in the end, do we really like or care about our own player character? Will we remember our nameless hero's escape from Site 2? After all, we are simply a guy with a gun who needed to shoot progressively bigger monsters as the game goes on.
Although it may seem as though the negatives are the only thing being explored in this review, that is only because these are the only deficiencies in my eyes, and once solved, this is would be not just an outstanding game, but an outstanding sequel. Right now it is definitely the former, but arguably not the latter. This game disappoints and exceeds expectation in equal measure. 
It has a beginning, middle and an end, with a solid if limited building system that fans of building games will enjoy to keep those inclined that way playing for a few hours more. But if the world of the Forest captivated you because of its outstanding story telling and environment design, this world may feel a bit cold and underwhelming. 
Six months on from its initial early access release, £25 buys you a fleshed out world with a strong enough story, deep enough gameplay and a badass shotgun*. With future updates and considerable content added since release, this is a game worth playing and keeping an eye on.
*unless you are using slugs. It feels like a giant pea shooter.

One of the best survival games to play with friends — AND THE GRAPHICS ARE ABSOLUTELY STUNNING!! Compared to the first game, this one is definitely an upgrade overall, though I still prefer some of the first game’s gameplay mechanics.

That said, had an absolute blast zooming around in the kart and smashing into cannibals alongside the hot, three-armed, four-legged baddy. Pure chaos!

Sons of the Forest is the most immersive horror game (your against cannibals, mutants and demons) and survival crafting game with the balance of a strong atmosphere and terrifying moments with player freedom. You also have AI companion like Kelvin who helps you in your base building and Virginia who will be like a body guard. After completing the story in multiplayer mode with both endings, it still keeps you invested in building multiple bases, and the most fun part exploring and surviving with your friends.

If you loved The Forest, the sequel takes everything that made the original great and turns it up a notch. It’s easily one of the most addictive survival games out there right now, successfully balancing genuine terror with absolute sandbox madness.

The game is a total chameleon depending on how you want to play. If you go in solo, it’s a brilliant, incredibly tense psychological horror. Every snapping twig in the woods will have you spinning around in a panic. But the second you hop on with friends, the vibe completely shifts into hilarious, chaotic fun. One minute you're trying to coordinate a base build, and the next you're laughing your heads off at the bizarre cannibal AI trying to raid your camp.

The dynamic seasons cycle is easily one of the best additions. Watching the island transition from a lush, sunny summer to a brutal, freezing winter isn't just eye candy; it completely changes the meta. It adds this amazing layer of unpredictability. A river that used to be a safe barrier and a great fishing spot suddenly freezes solid, meaning cannibals can just walk right across ice to get to you. You’re constantly forced to adapt, which keeps the gameplay loop feeling fresh.

That said, it definitely has some quirks that remind you it’s still a video game, for better or worse.

First off, nighttime lasts way too long. The pitch-black darkness is great for atmosphere initially, but it quickly crosses the line into tedious. You end up sitting around wasting resources just to see two feet in front of your face, which totally kills the momentum when you just want to build or explore.

Then there are the bugs and exploits that can completely break the survival tension if you let them. The biggest offender is an incredibly easy item dupe: all your friend has to do is put their items in storage, log out of the game, and log back in. When they spawn back in, their full inventory is magically restored, but the stuff they put in the boxes is still there. If your group lacks self-control, the scarcity mechanic goes right out the window.

Multiplayer progression can also feel a bit lazy in spots. Take the shovel, for instance. Only one person in the group actually needs to go get it. Since anything dug up by that player can be seen and grabbed by everyone else on the server, there's zero reason for the rest of the squad to bother grinding for their own. It kinda cheapens the reward of progression.

Even with the long nights and the goofy exploits, Sons of the Forest is a blast. It hits that perfect sweet spot between terrifying survival and total creative freedom. Just try to resist the urge to dupe an endless supply of shotgun shells on day two!

[h1] Review [/h1]
So... I'm back here to write a new review after-1.0 and after a 2 months break.

[h2] A real SURVIVAL HORROR Experience? [/h2]
This game has a beautiful graphic and this surely helps it to become one of the most good-looking videogames ever created. Sons Of The Forest is (or is not supposed to be) only this.

As the sequel of one of the most successfull SURVIVAL HORROR games, The Forest, Sons Of The Forest had a great responsibility: to be better than its predecessor. Too bad, some aspects, such as Survival and Horror, were not improved.

The game is supposed to be a SURVIVAL, but it's not so difficult for any player. The amount of MRE PACKS, SNACKS, CEREALS, CAT FOOD and SODAS makes the hunting system (that has not been changed since TF) completely useless. As many military/cannibals/guests camps are set around the whole island, you'll find a lot of resources that will last till the end of the game. There's no need to kill deers/moose/racoons as you have already everything in your inventory. You don't even need water as SODAS are everywhere found.
The real SURVIVAL EXPERIENCE happens only in late-game when you decide to stay on the island. Which, honesly, is not a great deal for all players. Only a bunch of them decide to stay and not finish the game, so...

The game was also supposed to be a HORROR. But, yet, the game is not scary: probably because of the need to show the new power of the lighting system in SOTF, caves are pretty lighten up, all torches you have (included the lighter) are more than enough to light up a dark area and you also find immediately a plastic torch in early game!
Surely mutants can be scary at the beginning but they won't be anymore after a third raid in 2 days. You get used to them and how to kill 'em in few minutes.

[h2] AI: An Alive World can be a Weak World [/h2]
Of course it is a good deal to give more... humanity to the in-game world. It's interesting how many relations cannibals can have while you're watching them, from drinking to rest, from training fighting each other to dance!

But this surely ruins the HORROR ASPECT, as they feel too human. Also the fact you have a lot of modern weapons pretty break the tension with the human threats and only mutants become a menace to deal with.

[h2] MODERN SURVIVAL? Or only MODERN SHOOTING? [/h2]
This game was never supposed to become what it is now. The modern stuff (and the easy way you can get all of it) destroyed the SURVIVAL ASPECT: too much food and beverage on a silver plate, too many vehicles that kill the feeling of the exploration, too many modern areas that don't look HORROR at all.

SOTF was supposed to be a MODERN SURVIVAL-HORROR GAME, but we got a MODERN HALF SURVIVAL FPS GAME. Surely it's still enjoyable but this is not what we have been told it was.

Overall, the gameplay is still very entertaining and enjoyable, may some mechanics are not really good for some but surely it can deliver a fun experience.


[h2] Overall, is it WORTH IT? Yes (but better with MODS) [/h2]
Absolutely yes. Not only this game has a beautiful graphic, but the easy mechanics and difficulties in the game can be a good deal for those players that were previously scared to play The Forest. The new AI, Modern Stuff and Resource System will deliver a new experience mainly focused on enjoying the gameplay and the beauty of the game while still having some challenges against the world, specifically the raids and the winter times. 

For those who look for an harder challenge, Sons Of The Forest has a large menu of MODS that really can change the way you play the game: from True Survival to RiseSpot, from RaidCustomizer to Planter Tweaks, the game will become way harder in terms of natural and human/mutant threats.
As someone who has played this game for a very long time, I found new challenges with MODS and a new way to play this game, a way it really changed the basics of surviving!

[h2] NOT A SCI-FI STORY (after all): that's the real twist! [/h2]
About the story, there are some problems (but that can be fixed by actually digging into it). And I say this as a fan of The Forest and Sons Of The Forest. I have slaughtered the games, opened the body and made autopsy to get the hell out of them and get what the story is and I now know how good it is... but not everyone will put as much effort into this, maybe only a few.

The fact is that, despite what happened in TF, SOTF really changes the way its predecessor paved with the main focus being on a SCI-FI story and drive into a new religious plot: the cultists, the Sons Of The Stars, the Sons Of Light, the artifacts, the Gold City (and also TF had many religious references that were later covered by the newer discoveries of the lab and the sci-fi twist behind the Vault)... there are so many elements that connect the game to the Bible and many other religious reference are set but too bad the player was expecting a completely different approach to the discovery of the Artifact Origins and all the community played it with that thought! That's why it appears the plot to be so weird and confusing. Everything is not explained and is sorrounded by that RELIGIOUS FOG that makes it hard to comprehend unless you dig into it and slaughter the body you'll find at the bottom of it. Which is what I suggest everyone to do!

Although my knowledge of the story is great, I can't oversee some evident issues:
- The main antagonist (Jianyu) spare you at the beginning without any actual reason and so will be throughout the entire plot.
- There is no urge to end the game even tho it's all focused on an event that is supposed to have specific time (you could wait years and still this even wouldnt happen because you didn't enter the final location) and this will also stuck many other NPCs and story characters.
- The story has an impressive depth and background that is poorly explained through notes and pickups that doesn't answer most of the questions (some will need your imagination or to look into details of environment design such as in Hell Cave).

I'm not saying the story is bad because it's impressive and I love it but the theory beauty doesn't stand in its execution. It seems something is missing and many answers do as well. Someone who doesn't know what The Forest is will also find difficult to explain some characters that might make 1, 2 appearences. Same happens with one (if not everyone) of the main characters that doesn't explain how he came on the island, how he managed to survive, what happened after a certain scene... There is so much this game could've been but it just isn't.

Hands down the best co op survival, base building, action exploration game ever made, there is so much to do, build, craft, explore and learn it boggles the mind. took me 30 hours just to complete the story.  

I don't want to even do a breakdown as it'll ruin the magic for a first time player, grab some friends and play this you won't regret it.

It's too good.
No other survival game I've played has this level of detail, immersion & intrigue all in one package.

Much more refined than the first game, with smoother gameplay and a ton of new weapons. The addition of companions adds a fresh dynamic, and the world feels even more immersive. However, the abundance of weapons does take away some of the scare factor, making it feel less intense than The Forest. Still, if you liked the first game, this one’s definitely worth diving into.

If you enjoyed The Forest, Sons of the Forest is a game you definitely shouldn't miss. The island’s design is much more complete and detailed, featuring wildlife and vegetation that feel alive and well-integrated, creating a highly believable and absorbing environment. Visually, the game is stunning. The graphics reach an impressive level of realism, with environments that look and feel incredibly satisfying, whether you're exploring dense forests or crossing snow-covered mountains. Every corner of the island feels carefully crafted, and it really shows during gameplay.

The cave system retains the spirit of the first game, with underground labyrinths that encourage exploration. However, in this installment, they feel somewhat underused: while their size is imposing and there are occasional enemy encounters, the constant sense of danger that defined The Forest is somewhat lost, as many caves feel empty or repetitive.

One of the game's strongest points is the building system. Personally, I love it. Unlike most other survival games, Sons of the Forest opts for a more realistic and intuitive approach, which adds an extra layer of satisfaction when constructing shelters and fortifications. Cutting down trees, designing structures piece by piece, and watching your base come to life feels natural and rewarding.

Not everything is perfect, though. Enemy AI is quite impressive but their strength borders on frustrating. Without armor, it's common to die in just three hits, which can disrupt the flow of exploration and construction. Additionally, crafting good armor feels tedious: despite being surrounded by a massive natural environment, natural protective gear (like wood) options are very limited. There's only the leaf armor, which is useful for stealth but offers very little combat protection. It would have been nice to see more types of armor crafted from natural resources.

Another aspect that doesn't quite shine is the story. Although the game presents a narrative that attempts to expand the island’s mystery, the plot feels secondary and not particularly impactful, far from being a true driving force to keep playing.

PROS:
+ Great visuals and scenery between the changing seasons
+ Combat mechanics and the clever AI of enemy NPC behaviour
+ Very immersive game of survival with consequences
+ Engaging building and upgrading
+ Kelvin and Virginia are helpful companions in gameplay

CONS:
- The game does not provide clear direction or guidance on where you need to go and what you need to do in order to progress the main story. The map markers are not clear or non-existent. This should be a setting to have on or off based on preference. Without the help of tutorials by the community, this game would be pretty much impossible to go through for the first time, as the tiniest unmarked details need to happen in a specific order or you end up wasting hours of your time running through woods or caves aimlessly just to find out you're missing something.

CONCLUSION:
Overall this is a very great game that I would recommend, but it is not one that I would replay again for the story, only for the free-roam, building, survival and combat.
